There's a particular quality to light in the late afternoon that painters have chased for centuries—the way it turns ordinary things golden, makes a brick wall or a parked car seem briefly significant. I find myself thinking about how much of what we call beauty is really just attention paid at the right moment.

Consider the humble pigeon. Most people barely register them, but look closely and you'll see iridescent feathers shifting from green to purple depending on the angle, a surprisingly intelligent eye, and a bird that has managed to thrive alongside humans in nearly every city on earth. Pigeons were once revered, carried messages across battlefields, and their ancestors were domesticated thousands of years ago. Now we mostly step around them. Nothing about the pigeon changed—only our willingness to notice.

I think about this with words too. "Window" comes from Old Norse, roughly meaning "wind-eye." Every window is a wind-eye, an opening the weather looks through. Once you know that, the word never sits quite the same again. Language is full of these buried images, small fossils of how people once saw the world.

Maybe that's what I'd want for anyone reading this: not grand revelations, just a slight tilt toward the unremarkable. The crack in the pavement where moss has taken hold. The specific sound rain makes on different surfaces. The fact that you're reading marks on a screen and hearing a voice in your head.

Ordinary things are inexhaustible. We just forget to look.
